alert_pattern: [FIRING:1] nfs critical (NFSConnectionCheckFailed aiware prod1 localhost:9100 node-exporter <IP> 2049 <region>)
diagnosis_steps: Map the alert IP to the NFS shard number and cloud instance ID; post 'Instance: <id>, IP: <ip>, Shard: <n>' in thread
Test the NFS port directly: nc -w 10 -v <IP> 2049 (times out when hung)
Check cloud instance status - 'Instance reachability check failed' has appeared with 99% CPU
If SSH works: systemctl status nfs-server && systemctl status aiware-agent
Check nfsd kernel threads: grep ^th /proc/net/rpc/nfsd (fleet default 80 has been repeatedly insufficient)
Check for hung processes: ps -eo state,pid,cmd | grep '^D' - 100+ nfsd processes in D state means NFS is hung; load average will sit at ~130
Check dmesg for 'nfsd: too many open connections, consider increasing the number of threads'
resolution_steps: If reachability failed, high CPU, or many D-state processes: REBOOT the instance (service restart will NOT recover hung nfsd - confirmed by senior engineer)
After boot verify nfs-server active and aiware-agent running; if the data path is not mounted, remount the data volume (check lsblk vs /etc/fstab) before starting nfs-server
Raise nfsd threads: rpc.nfsd 128, verify with grep ^th /proc/net/rpc/nfsd
Verify: nc -w 3 -v <IP> 2049 -> 'succeeded!'
Verify agent wrote its shard json (log line 'NFS - Successfully wrote .../nfs/<shard>.json')
Post outputs in thread; 'Alert resolved.'
gotchas: Alert commonly RE-FIRES within 1-2 hours if the box is degrading; monitor load after reboot, re-reboot if D-state processes accumulate again
systemctl restart of nfs-server/agent does not clear D-state hangs; only reboot does
On one occurrence the data volume did not remount at boot (exportfs: 'Failed to stat' the export path) - had to mount the data disk and swap device manually, then restart the agent

After an instance is recycled, shard reassignment bugs have occurred (instance re-registering with a different shard number, orphaning tasks assigned to the old shard). If jobs pile up on a shard with no active host, escalate to the edge platform team
Team has discussed OS upgrade as the structural fix for recurring nfsd hangs
escalation: Edge platform / senior SRE if shard mapping is inconsistent in the edge host table or jobs are stuck on a missing shard
example_commands: systemctl status nfs-server && systemctl status aiware-agent

alert_pattern: [FIRING:1] <cluster> : KubePersistentVolumeFillingUp - PVC <name> in <cluster> is only N% free
environment: any k8s cluster (seen on transcode scratch storage)
diagnosis_steps: Extract PVC name and namespace from alert (alert body includes 'PVC <name> filling up in <cluster>' and % free)
Confirm current usage on the storage dashboard; post the panel screenshot showing % free
Check whether the writer is a transcode/scratch workload - these fill during big jobs and MAY self-recover when the job completes
Check the runbook link embedded in the alert (Runbook: KubePersistentVolumeFillingUp - Resizing PVCs)
resolution_steps: Resize the PVC upward (observed: +50GB on a volume at ~8% free), per the resizing-PVCs runbook
Verify free space recovers (observed: 8% -> 39% free after adding 50GB)
Post the after screenshot in thread; resolved
gotchas: PVCs only grow, never shrink - size increases are permanent cost
Ack the VictorOps incident early so it doesn't escalate while you work
escalation: App owner if the same PVC needs resizing repeatedly (indicates a leak/retention problem, not capacity)

diagnosis_steps: Identify the target group (observed: the prod haproxy api http target group)
Check if the unhealthy target is a NEWLY LAUNCHED instance (autoscaling event) - post the target-health screenshot
resolution_steps: If newly launched: wait for warm-up; observed healthy within ~9 minutes with no action
Post the healthy-state screenshot; resolved
gotchas: Do not act in the first 5-10 minutes for fresh instances; most resolve on their own
If it stays unhealthy past warm-up, check the service on the health-check port and instance system log

environment: any nginx-fronted API env (seen on cloud gov clusters)
diagnosis_steps: Reproduce/spot-check: is the API returning 5xx right now (503 Service Temporarily Unavailable observed during incident)
Query the log platform for the window: upstreamStatus >= 500 and upstreamStatus <= 599; post sample log lines AND the search link in thread
Group errors by proxyUpstreamName to identify the failing service (observed: core graphql server, edge controller)
Count the ABSOLUTE number of 5xx (observed incident with only 19 total 5xx - threshold alerts can fire on small counts in low-traffic envs)
Correlate timing with pod restarts/rollouts of the upstream service
resolution_steps: If correlated with pod restarts: monitor until success rate recovers; document 'likely due to pods restarting'; resolved when 5xx stops
If sustained: investigate the specific upstream (logs, resources), consider scaling it
Post log excerpts + search links; resolved
gotchas: Status 531 with multi-GB requestSize = oversized client payload, not a platform fault
504 with latency exactly at the timeout ceiling (e.g. 300.002s) = upstream timeout - points at a slow backend call, not the proxy
Sanitize before sharing: raw nginx log lines contain live Bearer tokens - never paste them outside the incident thread
escalation: Service owner of the failing upstream if sustained
example_commands: kubectl get pods -n <ns> | grep <upstream> (check restart counts/ages)

alert_pattern: [FIRING:N] <cluster> : KubePodsNotReady (often N in the tens; engine pods)
environment: any aiWARE k8s cluster; usually engine pods
diagnosis_steps: List not-ready pods and bucket by state: kubectl get pods -n aiware | grep -vE 'Running|Completed' - states seen: ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff, Error, Pending/Init

ImagePullBackOff: verify the image tag actually exists in the registry (docker manifest inspect <image>); also check engine BUILD state - builds not in 'Deployed' state have caused pulls of unavailable images
Pending with FailedScheduling: read the event - node taints observed (ToBeDeletedByClusterAutoscaler, uninitialized, network-unavailable) usually mean node churn in progress
Error/CrashLoop: grep pod logs for the failure signature: panic|fatal|context deadline|Throttl|OOM|connection refused
Common crash signature: engine toolkit 'Failed to start subprocess [/opt/runner] err=context deadline exceeded' = engine couldn't reach the edge controller at startup
Check node health for the affected pods (kubectl describe node - pressure conditions, Ready history)
Check whether an ongoing change (cluster upgrade, controller rollout, load test) explains it - link the change thread
resolution_steps: Bulk-delete pods stuck in Error so the controller recreates them (observed 3500+ Error pods deleted at once)
If new pods immediately re-enter Error with the same log signature, deleting is futile - the dependency (edge controller / registry) is the problem; fix that first
For engine builds not Deployed: deploy the builds, pods recover
For autoscaler taint churn: usually self-heals as nodes finish cycling; monitor
Confirm backlogs drain after pods recover; resolved
gotchas: FIRING count is inflated - 50 crashlooping pods is usually ONE root cause (one engine build, one dependency, one node event)
If controller pods were rolled after the incident window, the relevant logs are gone - note it and move on rather than guessing
Deleting Error pods without checking the crash signature just burns scheduler cycles when the root cause persists
escalation: Engine/platform team when the crash is inside engine code or builds need redeployment
example_commands: kubectl get pods -n aiware --no-headers | grep eng | awk '{count[$3]++} END {for (s in count) print s, count[s]}'

alert_pattern: [FIRING:1] Wyvern - SQS Message Age DMH/DMH - prod pd (request queue, Seconds)
diagnosis_steps: Check queue depth/age trend - is it draining on its own?
Check with the app owner whether a known bulk workload is running (observed: customer re-runs / batch traffic explained the spike)
Check Wyvern ASG instance health/age
resolution_steps: Most occurrences: queue processes on its own within minutes - 'Queue processed. Alert resolved.'
If sustained: scale out the Wyvern ASG AND remove old/stale instances (both were needed in the sustained case); queue recovered after
Note: instance cycling during scale-out can briefly trigger a Processing Errors alert - expected, document it
gotchas: This alert flaps - it has re-fired minutes after resolving during bursts; check with the app owner before acting
Known-workload spikes (bulk re-processing) need no action, just a note in thread
escalation: App owner for load questions; infra for ASG scaling approval

diagnosis_steps: Identify server and drive letter from the alert (e.g. SQL41 R:, SQL43 I:)
Post current utilization % and absolute free GB in thread (e.g. '90%, 30GB free of 300GB')
This is a DB-owned system: notify/tag the DB owner before acting - NOC does not decide expansion alone
resolution_steps: Ask DB owner: cleanup or expand? (observed both: expand +100GB on approval; another case DB team cleaned up backup artifacts dropping 91.7% -> 50.7%)
If expansion approved: increase the disk, verify new utilization, post it
Resolved after utilization confirmed below threshold
gotchas: Recurring growth on the same drive has had an application root cause (backup artifacts, distribution DB growth) - the DB team investigates root cause in parallel; expansion is a stopgap
Response is slower than infra alerts because it waits on the DB owner - ack the incident to stop escalation
escalation: DB owner (required); their DB escalation rotation for the SQL servers

alert_pattern: Incident: AWS US (us-1) - Track Job / AWS SLED (us-gov-1) - Track Job (monitoring_tool: Runscope)
diagnosis_steps: Check the failing assertion in the Runscope test result (observed: "Status '500' was not a number equal to 200")
Run/await the next test execution - transient 5xx often passes on the subsequent run
Run the equivalent manual test (submit a job / API call) to confirm the platform actually works
resolution_steps: Most occurrences: subsequent automated test passes AND manual test passes -> document 'Manual test passed', resolved
If the manual test also fails: treat as a real API incident - pivot to the ApiSuccessRate playbook (5xx log investigation)
gotchas: Single-run Runscope failures are noisy; two consecutive failures or a failing manual test is the real signal
The same alert on multiple envs simultaneously suggests a shared dependency, not coincidence
escalation: None for transient; API on-call for confirmed failures

diagnosis_steps: Identify WHICH engine(s) have backlog and post engine name + ID + backlog size in thread

Pull recent task errors for that engine - error signatures observed: input asset 404 (bad jobs), unsupported input format sent by client, provider throttling (ProvisionedThroughputExceeded on cloud OCR), engine build too old for the input
Check pod health for that engine - if pods are fine, backlog is workload/task-level, not infra
Check for known causes: load testing in progress, bulk submissions, upstream change threads - link them
Identify the submitting org for bad-job floods (org ID from task records)
resolution_steps: Workload-explained (load test, bulk run): document the cause link, monitor drain, resolved
Bad input jobs (404 assets): confirm the asset URL actually 404s (HEAD request), then escalate to identify the submitter; engines are innocent
Provider throttling: backlog drains as retries succeed; flag quota increase to the cloud account owner
Engine-code failures: escalate to engine team (they may need to deploy newer builds); NOC cannot fix engine internals
'All pods running + backlog draining' cases: just monitor to completion
gotchas: Backlog alerts often accompany KubePodsNotReady on the same cluster - resolve pods first, backlog usually follows
A huge backlog of FAILING tasks (not slow ones) will not drain by waiting - an 'Engine failure rate above 15%' alert alongside means tasks are dying, not queued
Engineers outside NOC may only be able to diagnose, not fix (build deployments owned by another team) - set expectations in thread
escalation: Engine team for engine-internal failures; SRE for cluster-level causes; app owner for bad submissions

diagnosis_steps: Read the triggeredAlarm field: which alarm (CPU/memory), which VM/host/volume
Check whether the alarm coincides with a scheduled job (nightly backups have appeared inside the alarm text: 'Last Backup successfully completed at ...')
Check current host CPU/memory on the VMware dashboard
resolution_steps: Backup/scheduled-job spikes: self-resolve; observed incidents auto-resolved within ~10 minutes (RESOLVED_BY: SYSTEM)
Sustained red alarms outside job windows: check the VM workload with the app owner
gotchas: These frequently auto-resolve - the incident record often shows SYSTEM resolved it before anyone acted; don't over-invest in the first 10 minutes
Yellow (warning) variants of the same alarms are informational; track only if they recur

dashboard.name: 2. Windows Server Details Dashboard - With Services
dashboard.gotcha: Panel 21 filters on $instance (e.g. 10.60.4.182:9182), NOT on $hostname. The alert only gives the hostname, so set $hostname AND resolve $instance first, or the gauge renders a green 'N/A' that looks like a real reading.

diagnosis_steps: Translate the hostname the alert gives you into the instance the panel needs: windows_os_hostname{hostname="<HOST>"} returns instance=<ip>:9182.
Confirm the host actually reports memory before rendering: windows_os_physical_memory_free_bytes{instance="<ip>:9182"}. Zero series means no graph is possible for this host.
Render panel 21 with var-job=windows_exporter, var-hostname=<HOST>, var-instance=<ip>:9182.
Check whether the condition has already cleared — these often self-resolve before anyone looks.
resolution_steps: Read the graph: still climbing, flat, or already released?
If it has released, say so and recommend ack + resolve rather than opening an investigation.
If still high, identify what is holding the memory before recommending anything — the agent cannot see processes, only the metric.
gotchas: ONLY 21 OF 178 Windows hosts export the memory metric. Observed reporting: FTP, NY1WV5851, PowerBi3, SQL43, STG-ITAdmin, SVC144, SVC151, SVC158, SVC174, SVC175, SVC176, SVC182, SVC184, SVC187, SVC188, SVC70, Web30, Web31, Web32, Web33, ny1wv5852. If the alerting host is not one of these there is no graph to post — say that plainly instead of attaching an empty panel.
SVC183 specifically does NOT report memory, despite SVC182/184/187/188 all doing so.
This alert has no [FIRING:n] and no label group — the host is the bare token after the last ' - '. Do not look for Alertmanager labels.
The agent is read-only: it can show the graph, not free the memory.
